1: # Hausdorff dimension of a product with an interval
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi, *Real Analysis: Measure Theory,
6: Integration, and Hilbert Spaces*, Princeton Lectures in Analysis III,
7: Chapter 7, Problems, exercise 9, printed page 388.
8: Book DOI: [10.1515/9781400835560](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400835560).
9: 
10: > 9. Let \(E\) be a compact set in \(\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Show that
11: > \(\dim(E\times I)=\dim(E)+1\), where \(I\) is the unit interval in
12: > \(\mathbb R\).
13: 
14: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
15: 
16: Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
17: 2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
18: \(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
19: the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.
20: 
21: Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
22: compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
23: with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove
24: 
25: \[
26: \dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
27: \]
28: 
29: The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
30: formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
31: 
32: ## Fixed natural-language proof
33: 
34: For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put
35: 
36: \[
37: H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
38:  A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
39: \qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
40: \]
41: 
42: Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
43: unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension. We use
44: its critical-exponent characterization: \(H^s(A)=0\) if
45: \(s>\dim_H A\), and \(H^s(A)=\infty\) if \(0<s<\dim_H A\).
46: Conversely, zero measure implies \(\dim_H A\leq s\), and infinite
47: measure implies \(\dim_H A\geq s\).
48: 
49: Write \(D=\dim_H E\) and \(F=E\times[0,1]\). First \(0\leq D\leq n\).
50: Indeed, compactness makes \(E\) bounded. When \(n>0\), a box containing
51: it admits a cover by at most \(Ch^{-n}\) cubes of side at most \(h\),
52: for \(0<h\leq1\). Here \(C\) depends only on that box. Each cube has
53: diameter at most \(\sqrt n h\). For any \(s>n\), the total \(s\)-cost
54: is at most \(C n^{s/2}h^{s-n}\to0\). These arbitrarily fine covers
55: give \(H^s(E)=0\) and hence \(D\leq n\). If \(n=0\), nonemptiness
56: makes \(E=\mathbb R^0\), a singleton of zero \(s\)-cost for every
57: \(s>0\); thus \(D=0\).
58: 
59: ### Upper bound
60: 
61: When \(n=0\), \(F\) is isometric to \([0,1]\). Dividing this interval
62: into \(N\) equal pieces gives total \(a\)-cost \(N^{1-a}\to0\) for
63: every \(a>1\), proving \(\dim_H F\leq1=D+1\).
64: For this upper-bound argument now assume \(n\geq1\).
65: 
66: Fix \(q>D\). Since \(q>0\) and \(H^q(E)=0\), for every
67: \(0<r\leq1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a countable cover
68: \((U_i)\) of \(E\) with nonempty-member diameters
69: \(0<r_i\leq r\) and \(\sum_i r_i^q<\varepsilon\).
70: The positive-diameter requirement costs nothing: start with a cover of
71: cost below \(\varepsilon/2\); replace each zero-diameter singleton by
72: a ball of diameter at most \(r\), choosing the \(i\)-th replacement
73: to have \(q\)-cost less than \(\varepsilon2^{-i-2}\). The added cost
74: is less than \(\varepsilon/2\). Discard empty members.
75: 
76: Let \(N_i=\lceil1/r_i\rceil\). Partition \([0,1]\) into \(N_i\)
77: closed intervals of length \(1/N_i\leq r_i\). Because \(r_i\leq1\),
78: \(N_i\leq2/r_i\). The corresponding products with \(U_i\) form a
79: countable cover of \(F\). Each has Euclidean diameter at most
80: \(\sqrt2 r_i\), and their total \((q+1)\)-cost is at most
81: 
82: \[
83: \sum_iN_i(\sqrt2 r_i)^{q+1}
84: \leq2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\sum_i r_i^q
85: <2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\varepsilon.
86: \]
87: 
88: For any target scale \(\delta>0\), choose
89: \(r\leq\min(1,\delta/\sqrt2)\), then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
90: Thus \(H^{q+1}_\delta(F)=0\) for every scale, so
91: \(H^{q+1}(F)=0\) and \(\dim_H F\leq q+1\). Letting \(q\downarrow D\)
92: gives \(\dim_H F\leq D+1\).
93: 
94: ### Lower bound when \(D>0\)
95: 
96: Fix \(0<s<D\). Then \(H^s(E)=\infty\), so
97: \(H^s_\delta(E)\) becomes arbitrarily large as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
98: We claim that, for every \(\delta>0\),
99: 
100: \[
101: H^s_\delta(E)\leq H^{s+1}_\delta(F).                 \tag{1}
102: \]
103: 
104: Take an arbitrary countable \(\delta\)-cover \((V_i)_{i\geq0}\) of
105: \(F\), discarding empty members. Define
106: \(\rho_i=\operatorname{diam}V_i\),
107: \(A_i=\pi_{\mathbb R^n}(V_i)\), and
108: \(B_i=\pi_{\mathbb R}(V_i)\). Coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz,
109: so both projected diameters are at most \(\rho_i\leq\delta\).
110: For \(\varepsilon>0\), put
111: 
112: \[
113: \eta_i=\frac{\varepsilon2^{-i-1}}{1+\rho_i^s}>0.
114: \]
115: 
116: Enclose \(B_i\) in an open interval \(J_i\) of length at most
117: \(\rho_i+\eta_i\): its supremum minus infimum is at most \(\rho_i\),
118: and an enlargement of total width \(\eta_i\) suffices. This avoids
119: assuming that the arbitrary covering sets or their projections are measurable.
120: 
121: For each \(t\in[0,1]\), the sets \(A_i\) for which \(t\in J_i\)
122: cover \(E\). Indeed, a point \((x,t)\in F\) belongs to some \(V_i\),
123: giving \(x\in A_i\) and \(t\in B_i\subset J_i\). Their diameters
124: are at most \(\rho_i\). Consequently, with \(c=H^s_\delta(E)\),
125: 
126: \[
127: c\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s\mathbf1_{J_i}(t)\quad(t\in[0,1]).
128: \]
129: 
130: The constant \(c\) is finite: compactness gives a finite cover of \(E\)
131: by balls of diameter at most \(\delta\), with finite \(s\)-cost.
132: Each summand is nonnegative and measurable since \(J_i\) is open.
133: Integrate over \([0,1]\), of Lebesgue measure one, and use Tonelli's
134: theorem for this nonnegative series. Since
135: \(|J_i\cap[0,1]|\leq\rho_i+\eta_i\),
136: 
137: \[
138: \begin{aligned}
139: c&\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s|J_i\cap[0,1]|\\
140:  &\leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\sum_i\eta_i\rho_i^s
141:  \leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\varepsilon.
142: \end{aligned}
143: \]
144: 
145: If the first series is infinite the desired inequality is immediate;
146: otherwise let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Take the infimum over the
147: arbitrary covers to obtain (1). As its left side is unbounded at small
148: scales, \(H^{s+1}(F)=\infty\), giving \(\dim_H F\geq s+1\).
149: Letting \(s\uparrow D\) proves \(\dim_H F\geq D+1\).
150: 
151: ### Lower bound when \(D=0\)
152: 
153: Choose \(x_0\in E\). The map \(t\mapsto(x_0,t)\) is an isometric
154: embedding of \([0,1]\) into \(F\), so dimension monotonicity gives
155: \(\dim_H F\geq\dim_H[0,1]\). This interval has dimension one:
156: equal-length covers gave the upper bound above. For \(0<s<1\), any
157: \(\delta\)-cover with diameters \(\rho_i\leq\delta\) satisfies
158: \(\sum_i\rho_i\geq1\). To see this, enclose its nonempty members
159: in open intervals of lengths at most \(\rho_i+\varepsilon2^{-i-1}\),
160: use countable subadditivity of length to get
161: \(1\leq\sum_i\rho_i+\varepsilon\), and let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
162: Hence \(\sum_i\rho_i^s\geq\delta^{s-1}\sum_i\rho_i
163: \geq\delta^{s-1}\to\infty\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
164: This proves the lower bound one. Thus \(\dim_H F\geq1=D+1\),
165: including when \(n=0\).
166: 
167: Together the bounds establish the required equality.
168: 
169: ## Input status
170:

definitions.type: family, indexed by k∈ℕ, of Euclidean metric spaces
definitions.definition: Eucl(k)=ℝ^k, the real coordinate vectors indexed by {0,...,k−1}, with distance dist(x,y)=(∑_{j<k}(x_j−y_j)^2)^(1/2). Eucl(0) consists of the empty vector. On Eucl(k)×ℝ we use dist((x,t),(y,u))=(dist(x,y)^2+|t−u|^2)^(1/2), identified with Eucl(k+1) by appending the last coordinate; no maximum product metric is used. Balls mean {y:dist(x,y)<a}. All these spaces carry the topology of this metric and its Borel measurable structure.

definitions.type: extended nonnegative diameter of a subset of a metric or extended metric space
definitions.definition: For a subset A of a metric or extended metric space X, diam(A)=sup{d(x,y):x,y∈A} in [0,∞], where d is its (extended) distance and sup∅=0. Thus diam∅=0. When diam(A)≤a<∞ we treat it as the corresponding finite nonnegative real number. Countable sums of nonnegative quantities mean the supremum of finite partial sums, and may be infinite; powers with positive exponent have 0^s=0 and ∞^s=∞.

definitions.type: Hausdorff content and measure functions on Euclidean sets with positive real exponent
definitions.definition: For every k∈ℕ, A⊆Eucl(k), s>0 and δ>0, H^s_δ(A)=inf{∑_{i≥0}(diam U_i)^s : (U_i) is a countable cover of A and diam U_i≤δ for every i}, and H^s(A)=sup_{δ>0} H^s_δ(A), with values in [0,∞]. Finite covers are allowed by padding with empty sets; empty members contribute zero. The infimum of an empty collection is ∞. This is exactly the unnormalized diameter-power convention of problem.md:34–42.

definitions.type: pair of native Hausdorff measure and dimension constructions on an extended metric space
definitions.definition: For an extended metric space X with its Borel measurable structure, Native(X).measure(σ) denotes MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure σ, defined in the pinned library as Measure.mkMetric(r↦r^σ). Here mkMetric forms, for each positive extended radius, the covering outer measure with cost r^σ of the extended diameter for nonempty sets (empty sets cost zero), and takes their supremum as the radius decreases to zero, with the Borel measure structure. Evaluations on arbitrary sets mean outer measure evaluations, without requiring those sets measurable. Extended powers use the native ENNReal.rpow convention, including r^0=1. Native(X).dimension(A) denotes dimH A, defined as sup over a∈[0,∞) with Native(X).measure(a)(A)=∞ of the extended nonnegative number a; an empty supremum is zero. This names the exact native definitions, not an assertion about H.

binders.type: extended metric space with its Borel measurable structure

definitions.type: extended nonnegative Hausdorff dimension of Euclidean sets
definitions.definition: For k∈ℕ and A⊆Eucl(k), dim_H(A)=Native(Eucl(k)).dimension(A), the usual Hausdorff dimension, valued in [0,∞]. In particular the empty set has dimension zero by this definition. No finiteness is imposed by this definition; finiteness of the dimensions occurring in the target is proved below.

I=[0,1]={t∈ℝ:0≤t≤1}. When I or a subset of the real line is an argument of H or dim_H, it is identified with the subset of Eucl(1) obtained by t↦(t), the one-coordinate vector; this map has distance sqrt((t−u)^2)=|t−u|. Thus all diameter, cover and dimension notation for real subsets uses exactly their usual real-line metric. In λ(I) and real integrals I is the real interval itself.
F=E×I={(x,t):x∈E,t∈I}, regarded as a subset of Eucl(n+1) under D001's coordinate-appending Euclidean isometry.
D=dim_H(E). Finiteness and 0≤D≤n are conclusions, not assumptions.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on the Borel real line, evaluated as an outer measure on arbitrary sets
definitions.definition: λ is the usual Lebesgue measure MeasureTheory.volume on ℝ. For any nonnegative extended-real function f, ∫f dλ denotes its nonnegative Lebesgue integral (the supremum of the integrals of nonnegative measurable simple functions bounded above by f). For a set B and constant c≥0, c 1_B is c on B and zero outside B. For a bounded open interval J=(a,b) with a<b its length |J| means b−a.

The dimension in D005 is exactly the native dimension, and is nonnegative since it takes values in [0,∞]. Under s>0, s defines a nonnegative real source exponent. For positive δ, decreasing δ restricts the admissible covers and therefore increases their infimum. All costs are nonnegative. If H^s(A)=0, every scale infimum is zero. By the defining greatest-lower-bound property, for every positive threshold a cover has cost below it: otherwise that positive threshold would be a lower bound. H002 and M012 imply that E is bounded in the Euclidean metric bornology.
